Four applied outcomes that you will practice in the hands-on activity and runtime wiring.

screens.title: What the Config trait is and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: The Config trait is the contract a pallet exposes to the runtime so the runtime can provide concrete types and constants. Think of it as a set of plugs and dials. The pallet declares type placeholders like Balance or Event and constants such as MaxItemsPerUser. The runtime implements Config for the pallet and supplies the actual numeric types or values. This separation is essential because it prevents hardcoding deployment-specific details inside the pallet, which would otherwise require editing and recompiling the pallet for each chain. A concrete example is a token pallet that declares type Balance; one runtime may set Balance = u128 while another might choose u64. Similarly, constants marked with #[pallet::constant] become runtime constants that other pallets and the UI can query. A common misconception is to use StorageValue for values that never change; if a parameter belongs to deployment configuration, prefer defining it in Config so the runtime clearly documents it. Key teaching: treat Config as the pallet's external interface for types and static parameters. How would you decide whether a value belongs in Config or should be on-chain mutable storage?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Config Trait
Definition

Config trait

A contract of associated types and constants the runtime fills in. It is how the pallet declares dependencies on runtime-provided items.

Why it matters
Keeps logic generic, enables reuse across chains, and exposes compile-time guarantees for types.
Misconception
Don't confuse Config constants with mutable on-chain parameters; Config values represent deployment choices, not necessarily governance-controlled storage.
Key Takeaway

Use Config to declare the surface your pallet needs from the runtime and avoid embedding deployment details in logic.

Example
<!-- Escaped Rust example -->
pub trait Config: frame_system::Config {
    type Event: From<Event<Self>> + Into<<Self as frame_system::Config>::Event>;
    type Balance: Parameter + Member + AtLeast32BitUnsigned + Codec + Default + Copy + MaybeSerializeDebug;
    #[pallet::constant]
    type MinTransferAmount: Get<Self::Balance>;
    #[pallet::constant]
    type MaxItemsPerUser: Get<u32>;
}
Use in code
Refer to T::Balance and T::MaxItemsPerUser::get() to access runtime settings.
Pro-tip
Mark items you expect the runtime to expose as #[pallet::constant] when they should be readable across the runtime and UI.

screens.title: Using associated types in pallet logic
screens.narratorSegment: Associated types and constants become the building blocks you use inside your pallet's functions. When you write a dispatchable that takes a value of type T::Balance, you are asserting the runtime will provide a concrete numeric type that satisfies the trait bounds declared in Config. For constants, the pattern T::MaxItemsPerUser::get() returns the runtime value at compile time through the Get trait. A concrete example from the chapter is a do_something dispatchable that ensures a transferred value is above a MinTransferAmount and that the sender does not exceed MaxItemsPerUser. Using these checks preserves invariants and prevents faulty state transitions. A common pitfall is attempting to cast or assume widths for balance types without respecting the trait bounds; always rely on the trait constraints and Get where provided. The code panel shows both the Config declaration and the dispatchable snippet; read the code to see how ensure! is used with T::MinTransferAmount::get() and how storage access uses storage maps parameterized by T. Closing question: how would you change behavior if you wanted governance to update a parameter after genesis? Using associated types in pallet logic means use t::type for type-correct values and t::constant::get() to read deployment constants inside dispatchables.. In practical terms, how t::type and t::constant::get() appear in dispatchables and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Using Config Items
Dispatchable example
<!-- Escaped Rust example -->
#[weight = 10_000]
pub fn do_something(origin, value: T::Balance) -> DispatchResult {
    let sender = ensure_signed(origin)?;
    ensure!(value >= T::MinTransferAmount::get(), Error::ValueTooLow);
    let current_items = <Items<T>>::get(&sender).len();
    ensure!(current_items < T::MaxItemsPerUser::get() as usize, Error::TooManyItems);
    Ok(())
}
Notice how ensure! uses the Get trait for constants and how types are expressed as T::Balance so they match the runtime's concrete type.
Explanation
  • Ensure checks use T::MinTransferAmount::get() to enforce runtime-provided thresholds.
  • Storage access like <Items<T>> is typed to the pallet's Config so maps carry correct AccountId and item types.
  • If you need mutable parameters after launch, expose storage and a governance-controlled setter rather than baking them into Config alone.
Common mistake
Assuming all chains will use the same numeric width for Balance; rely on the Config trait bounds instead of casting arbitrarily.

screens.title: Hardcoding vs Config — tradeoffs
screens.narratorSegment: A common decision point is whether to hardcode a value inside a pallet or expose it via the Config trait. Hardcoding is tempting because it's simple, but it couples the pallet to a single deployment. If the value must change, you would need to modify code, recompile the runtime, and perform a hard fork. This is expensive and risky. The Config approach keeps the logic generic; the runtime selects types and constants at compile time without touching the pallet code. For example, if an interest rate or a maximum name length should vary across deployments, declare them in Config. There are tradeoffs: if a parameter truly must be mutable in operation, then you might store it in StorageValue and provide governance-controlled setters; Config is for deployment-time choices and compile-time type guarantees. A useful mental model is: use Config for deployment wiring and Storage for runtime-controlled state. Misconception to avoid: believing that Config is how to enable end-user updates — that's not its purpose. Closing reflection: which of your project's parameters are stable deployment choices and which require on-chain governance? Hardcoding vs Config — tradeoffs means config is for deployment-time values and types; storage is for mutable, governance-driven parameters.. In practical terms, why configured parameters beat baked-in constants for reusable pallets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Hardcoding vs Config
Hardcoding
Pros and cons
  • Pros: simple to implement initially, fewer moving parts.
  • Cons: inflexible, requires runtime recompilation and hard fork to change, reduces reusability.
  • Example mistake: embedding a fixed interest rate inside pallet logic.
Avoid for values that might vary across deployments.
Config
Pros and cons
  • Pros: reusable pallet, runtime author chooses types and constants, clearer separation of concerns.
  • Cons: values are fixed at compile-time unless paired with on-chain storage and governance for runtime changes.
  • Example pattern: type Balance and MaxItemsPerUser supplied by runtime implementer.
Prefer Config for deployment configuration and type guarantees.
Check your understanding

If you need to let token holders vote on a parameter after launch, would you put it in Config or Storage? Why?

screens.title: What Genesis Storage is and when to use it
screens.narratorSegment: Genesis Storage is the initial persistent state the chain uses at block zero. It is how you pre-populate StorageValue, StorageMap, and StorageDoubleMap entries so important accounts, balances, or roles exist from the first block. You use Genesis storage when initial state matters for security, usability, or correctness — for example pre-allocating tokens to a treasury and developer fund or pre-registering names in a registry pallet. Without GenesisConfig, operators would have to submit transactions after launch to set critical data, which is error-prone and could be less secure. To implement genesis seeding in a pallet, declare a GenesisConfig struct inside decl_storage! and implement GenesisBuild<T> to copy values from the struct into storage maps during runtime initialization. A typical pattern includes providing Default for GenesisConfig to make runtime defaults sensible. Misconception: GenesisConfig is not a runtime governance tool — it's a one-off initialization step. Closing question: which values in your project must be present at genesis and cannot wait for user transactions? What Genesis Storage is and when to use it means genesis storage seeds the chain's initial state so critical values and accounts exist from block zero.. In practical terms, seed maps, values, and roles at chain launch to avoid manual setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Genesis Storage

Genesis Storage explained

Use GenesisConfig to supply initial storage so the chain boots with required accounts, balances, or roles without manual transactions.

When to use
Pre-allocations, admin roles, or any state that must exist from block zero.
Misconception
GenesisConfig is not for runtime parameter changes after launch. It runs once during initialization.
Key Takeaway

Seed critical state at genesis to avoid manual and insecure post-launch initialization.

Concrete example
Pre-allocate tokens: supply a vector of (AccountId, Balance) in a Balances::GenesisConfig so treasury and developer fund receive tokens at genesis. The build_storage implementation then inserts each pair into the Balances map.
<!-- Escaped Rust snippet -->
GenesisConfig {
  balances: Vec<(T::AccountId, T::Balance)>,
}

impl GenesisBuild<T> for GenesisConfig {
  fn build_storage(&self) -> Result<, sp_runtime::BuildStorageError> {
    for (who, balance) in &self.balances {
      <Balances<T>>::insert(who, balance);
    }
    Ok(())
  }
}

screens.title: Implementing GenesisConfig inside a pallet
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing GenesisConfig follows a small sequence of steps you perform inside decl_storage!. First, declare the GenesisConfig struct to hold the initial values your pallet needs, such as a Vec of (AccountId, Balance) or a Vec of (Vec, AccountId) for a registry. Second, implement Default for GenesisConfig so the runtime has a sensible fallback when integrators omit values. Default helps local testing and keeps the runtime's top-level GenesisConfig construction ergonomic. Third, implement GenesisBuild<T> for the GenesisConfig and implement build_storage to copy the values into the pallet's storage maps and values. In build_storage you iterate through the provided initial data and call <StorageMap<T>>::insert for each pair. It is critical to ensure the data you place in genesis is internally consistent — for example, balances should not exceed an expected total if your logic depends on total supply. A typical mistake is forgetting to insert both forward and reverse map entries when a pallet uses two maps to keep bidirectional lookups; always seed both maps if your runtime expects them. How would you test your build_storage before publishing? Implementing GenesisConfig inside a pallet means declare genesisconfig, provide default, and implement genesisbuild::build_storage to seed storage safely.. In practical terms, declare, default, and build the genesis struct. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Example build_storage implementation
screens.narratorSegment: A typical build_storage implementation iterates an initial vector of pairs and inserts each pair into one or more storage maps. For a registry that keeps both an account-to-name map and a name-to-account reverse map, you must insert entries into both Maps. The code example in the chapter demonstrates exactly this pattern: inside impl GenesisBuild<T> for GenesisConfig, the build_storage function loops through self. initial_names and calls <Names<T>>::insert(who, name) and <NameOwners<T>>::insert(name, who). Pay attention to ownership and borrowing: the example iterates references and uses the storage insert A P I to copy values into runtime storage. A common error is inserting only one side of a bidirectional mapping, which leaves the runtime inconsistent and can cause lookups to fail. To test, include both maps in integration tests and verify lookups return the expected owners and names. Closing question: if two genesis entries conflict (same name, different owner), how should your build_storage handle it? Example build_storage implementation means loop through genesisconfig entries and insert both forward and reverse map entries to maintain consistent lookups at genesis.. In practical terms, iterate initial pairs and insert into storagemap and reverse map. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: A typical build_storage implementation iterates an initial vector of pairs and inserts each pair into one or more storage maps. For a registry that keeps both an account-to-name map and a name-to-account reverse map, you must insert entries into both Maps. The code example in the chapter demonstrates exactly this pattern: inside impl GenesisBuild<T> for GenesisConfig, the build_storage function loops through self. initial_names and calls <Names<T>>::insert(who, name) and <NameOwners<T>>::insert(name, who). Pay attention to ownership and borrowing: the example iterates references and uses the storage insert A P I to copy values into runtime storage. A common error is inserting only one side of a bidirectional mapping, which leaves the runtime inconsistent and can cause lookups to fail. To test, include both maps in integration tests and verify lookups return the expected owners and names. Closing question: if two genesis entries conflict (same name, different owner), how should your build_storage handle it? Example build_storage implementation means loop through genesisconfig entries and insert both forward and reverse map entries to maintain consistent lookups at genesis.. In practical terms, iterate initial pairs and insert into storagemap and reverse map. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › build_storage Example
Example code
<!-- Escaped Rust snippet -->
impl GenesisBuild<T> for GenesisConfig {
    fn build_storage(&self) -> Result<, sp_runtime::BuildStorageError> {
        for (name, owner) in &self.initial_names {
            <Names<T>>::insert(owner, name);
            <NameOwners<T>>::insert(name, owner);
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
Example scenario
Pre-register Alice and Bob so their names resolve at genesis without transactions.
Common mistake
Inserting only into one map and forgetting the reverse mapping breaks uniqueness checks and lookups.

Seed both forward and reverse storage entries if your pallet relies on bidirectional lookups at runtime.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize six core terms and why each matters. First, the Config trait is your pallet's interface for the runtime to provide types and constants; it enables reuse and decoupling. Second, Associated Types are placeholders like Balance that the runtime must concretely implement, ensuring type correctness in pallet logic. Third, Associated Constants allow the runtime to provide deployment-specific numeric parameters, often exposed with #[pallet::constant] so other pallets and the UI can query them. Fourth, Genesis Storage is the chain's initial state at block zero and is used to seed critical data like allocations or admin roles. Fifth, the GenesisConfig struct holds the initial values for a pallet's storage items and should implement Default for sensible runtime defaults. Sixth, the GenesisBuild<T> trait contains build_storage, the function that copies entries from GenesisConfig into on-chain storage during initialization. These concise definitions are the mental checklist you should use when designing configurable, deployable pallets.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn two linked capabilities that make Substrate pallets practical in real deployments. First, the Config trait lets a pallet declare its configurable types and constants so a runtime can set concrete types like Balance or values like a maximum length. This avoids brittle, hardcoded values and makes pallets reusable across different chains. Second, Genesis storage and the GenesisConfig pattern let you pre-populate storage items when the chain first starts. That is essential for pre-allocations, initial roles, or seeding registries without manual transactions. A concrete example you will see in the hands-on activity is a registry pallet where the maximum name length is provided by Config and some names are pre-registered through GenesisConfig. You will explore how to define associated types and constants, annotate constants with the pallet constant attribute, implement GenesisBuild to insert initial map entries, and wire the pallet into the runtime's lib. rs so the build step runs at genesis. By the end, you will be able to both parameterize a pallet and reliably set its initial state. Consider: what deployment parameters in your real project should be configurable versus baked in?

Over the next screens you will gain four practical competencies. First, you will learn to make a pallet configurable by defining a Config trait with associated types and constants, and you will understand why that keeps logic generic and reusable. Second, you will implement concrete type bindings and constants in a runtime so a pallet can use T::X values safely at compile time. Third, you will learn the GenesisConfig pattern: how to declare a genesis struct, implement Default for sensible defaults, and implement GenesisBuild so build_storage populates storage maps and values before the chain runs. Fourth, you will integrate the genesis configuration into the runtime's lib. rs so the chain orchestration invokes your pallet's genesis builder. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or visual to help you remember: trait = plug, genesis = seed, runtime = wiring, build_storage = installer. These skills matter because they let you ship pallets that work in different deployments and boot with a secure initial state. As you progress, reflect on which parameters in your own project should be configurable and which state must exist at genesis.

This second objectives screen frames the same four outcomes as applied tasks you will perform. You will first create a Config trait entry such as a MaxNameLength constant and a Balance type so the runtime picks a concrete number type. Next, you will enforce those values inside a dispatchable; for example, ensure! checks that a user-provided name is not longer than the MaxNameLength provided by the runtime. Third, you will author a GenesisConfig that holds a collection of initial pairs to insert into a StorageMap so a registry starts with pre-registered names. Finally, you will wire your pallet into the runtime's lib. rs and place your GenesisConfig into the runtime-wide GenesisConfig so frame_system calls your build step at genesis. Each applied objective includes a small mnemonic: plug the type, enforce at runtime, seed values at genesis, and wire into the runtime. This applied framing helps you move from reading code to producing a deployable runtime with predictable initial state.

The Config trait is the contract a pallet exposes to the runtime so the runtime can provide concrete types and constants. Think of it as a set of plugs and dials. The pallet declares type placeholders like Balance or Event and constants such as MaxItemsPerUser. The runtime implements Config for the pallet and supplies the actual numeric types or values. This separation is essential because it prevents hardcoding deployment-specific details inside the pallet, which would otherwise require editing and recompiling the pallet for each chain. A concrete example is a token pallet that declares type Balance; one runtime may set Balance = u128 while another might choose u64. Similarly, constants marked with #[pallet::constant] become runtime constants that other pallets and the UI can query. A common misconception is to use StorageValue for values that never change; if a parameter belongs to deployment configuration, prefer defining it in Config so the runtime clearly documents it. Key teaching: treat Config as the pallet's external interface for types and static parameters. How would you decide whether a value belongs in Config or should be on-chain mutable storage?

Associated types and constants become the building blocks you use inside your pallet's functions. When you write a dispatchable that takes a value of type T::Balance, you are asserting the runtime will provide a concrete numeric type that satisfies the trait bounds declared in Config. For constants, the pattern T::MaxItemsPerUser::get() returns the runtime value at compile time through the Get trait. A concrete example from the chapter is a do_something dispatchable that ensures a transferred value is above a MinTransferAmount and that the sender does not exceed MaxItemsPerUser. Using these checks preserves invariants and prevents faulty state transitions. A common pitfall is attempting to cast or assume widths for balance types without respecting the trait bounds; always rely on the trait constraints and Get where provided. The code panel shows both the Config declaration and the dispatchable snippet; read the code to see how ensure! is used with T::MinTransferAmount::get() and how storage access uses storage maps parameterized by T. Closing question: how would you change behavior if you wanted governance to update a parameter after genesis? Using associated types in pallet logic means use t::type for type-correct values and t::constant::get() to read deployment constants inside dispatchables.. In practical terms, how t::type and t::constant::get() appear in dispatchables and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common decision point is whether to hardcode a value inside a pallet or expose it via the Config trait. Hardcoding is tempting because it's simple, but it couples the pallet to a single deployment. If the value must change, you would need to modify code, recompile the runtime, and perform a hard fork. This is expensive and risky. The Config approach keeps the logic generic; the runtime selects types and constants at compile time without touching the pallet code. For example, if an interest rate or a maximum name length should vary across deployments, declare them in Config. There are tradeoffs: if a parameter truly must be mutable in operation, then you might store it in StorageValue and provide governance-controlled setters; Config is for deployment-time choices and compile-time type guarantees. A useful mental model is: use Config for deployment wiring and Storage for runtime-controlled state. Misconception to avoid: believing that Config is how to enable end-user updates — that's not its purpose. Closing reflection: which of your project's parameters are stable deployment choices and which require on-chain governance? Hardcoding vs Config — tradeoffs means config is for deployment-time values and types; storage is for mutable, governance-driven parameters.. In practical terms, why configured parameters beat baked-in constants for reusable pallets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Genesis Storage is the initial persistent state the chain uses at block zero. It is how you pre-populate StorageValue, StorageMap, and StorageDoubleMap entries so important accounts, balances, or roles exist from the first block. You use Genesis storage when initial state matters for security, usability, or correctness — for example pre-allocating tokens to a treasury and developer fund or pre-registering names in a registry pallet. Without GenesisConfig, operators would have to submit transactions after launch to set critical data, which is error-prone and could be less secure. To implement genesis seeding in a pallet, declare a GenesisConfig struct inside decl_storage! and implement GenesisBuild<T> to copy values from the struct into storage maps during runtime initialization. A typical pattern includes providing Default for GenesisConfig to make runtime defaults sensible. Misconception: GenesisConfig is not a runtime governance tool — it's a one-off initialization step. Closing question: which values in your project must be present at genesis and cannot wait for user transactions? What Genesis Storage is and when to use it means genesis storage seeds the chain's initial state so critical values and accounts exist from block zero.. Let's summarize six core terms and why each matters. First, the Config trait is your pallet's interface for the runtime to provide types and constants; it enables reuse and decoupling. Second, Associated Types are placeholders like Balance that the runtime must concretely implement, ensuring type correctness in pallet logic. Third, Associated Constants allow the runtime to provide deployment-specific numeric parameters, often exposed with #[pallet::constant] so other pallets and the UI can query them. Fourth, Genesis Storage is the chain's initial state at block zero and is used to seed critical data like allocations or admin roles. Fifth, the GenesisConfig struct holds the initial values for a pallet's storage items and should implement Default for sensible runtime defaults. Sixth, the GenesisBuild<T> trait contains build_storage, the function that copies entries from GenesisConfig into on-chain storage during initialization. These concise definitions are the mental checklist you should use when designing configurable, deployable pallets.

These final reminders tie the chapter into practical next steps. First, mark constants you expect the runtime to expose with #[pallet::constant] so they become runtime constants other pallets and UIs can read. Second, prefer Config for deployment-specific choices and Storage with governance setters for runtime-mutable parameters. Third, when seeding maps in build_storage, always check for duplicate keys and maintain invariants such as total supply limits. Fourth, include sensible Default implementations for GenesisConfig to make development and CI convenient. Fifth, test thoroughly by running a local dev node and inspecting initial state in Polkadot-JS Apps or similar tools. Finally, when integrating into a runtime, ensure that construct_runtime! includes your pallet's GenesisConfig so the system runs your build_storage at genesis. Keep these practical items as a deployment checklist when preparing a pallet for distribution or inclusion in a chain's runtime.
